## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.76640.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.76640.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cd59 and inflammation orchestrate Schwann cell development" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

There is strong consensus by all three reviewers on the potential interest and novelty of the paper. However, reviewers 1 and 3 felt that more experiments are needed to support the major conclusions of the paper. I do agree with these reviewers that the data in figure 2, 3 and 5 should be significantly improved to be more convincing. I also agree that, while the rescue is impressive, desametazone has very broad action and more data are needed to corroborate that excessive proliferation and myelination were actually rescued after desametazone treatment. Although the suggestion of reviewer 1 to confirm the rescue using available drugs with a more restricted complement effect is valuable, I think that it would be sufficient to discuss the shortcoming of desametazone and tune down the claims about the effect of inflammation in the text and title. Reviewers 1 and 3 also had questions about the mechanisms, that relate to explanation regarding the large effect of Cd59 deletion, given the small percentage of cells expressing CD59, and also on how to explain the relationship between Schwann cell proliferation and impaired myelination or formation of nodes of Ranvier. I would add to this that it is very surprising that increased proliferation in Schwann cell precursors does not lead to increased apoptosis, as it is well known that Schwann cell precursors depend on axonal contact for survival.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. What could impair myelination if Schwann cells are not overproliferating anymore at the time of myelination? Analysis of the Schwann cell cycle at the time of myelination could provide some explanation. We need at least expression data of the inducers and inhibitors of myelination. There is also no functional analyses. The impaired myelination and node of Ranvier formation must lead to functional impairment.

2. Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel C: even with a lot of effort, I cannot see co-localization of cd59 (cyan) with Sox10:megfp (orange) at any time-point. It could be that some of the Sox10:megfp-labeled cells are cd59-positive, but arrows are missing on the orange channel and it is not clear whether those are confocal images or not. Whether cd59 is expressed in Sox10-expressing cells is an essential point for the study, so it is important to show convincing images. Co-localization is also not convincing in Figure 2B. In addition, the arrows seem to indicate cd59-positive cells and not Sox10:megfp SCs or OLs, as stated in the figure legend. Co-IF showing cd59:tagrfp expression in Sox10-positive SCs is more convincing. Please, add co-IF images at 3 or 4 dpf to illustrate quantification shown in Figure 2E. According to the Material and methods section, the IF images seem to have been taken by confocal microscopy. Please, add this information in the figure legend.

3. Figure 2¬—figure supplement 2: in panel A, co-localization is again not obvious at all. In panels B-D, what are we looking at? IF or in vivo labeling? Could the authors quickly clarify the expected subcellular localization of the different egfp reporters used here to avoid the need to look for this information in the referenced articles?

4. Figure 3G: same comment as above, not convincing. I really do not understand what we are looking at. In Figure 3H, the authors show a graph representing the number of puncta per cell. Does it mean that what is shown in Figure 3G is a single cell? To me, this does not look like a single cell. How do the authors define the limits of single cells? They need to show images with several cells so that we have an idea of how straightforward it is to detect the limits of each cell. In the figure legend of Figure 3G, it is not written that the images presented show single cells.

5. Figure 5A: THE EM images of the mutant and the control look very different in quality. Could the authors show images of comparable quality/resolution? Looking at these images, I wonder how easy it is to count individual wraps in a reliable manner. In Figure 5D, it seems that the total number of axons has been used as n for statistics and not the average of all axons per fish with a n of 3, as stated in the figure legend. For statistical analyses, the n should be the number of fish, n=3. If the n is too high, there is a risk of finding a significant difference where there is no real difference. Please, re-calculate in case the n used was indeed the number of axons and not the number of fish.

6. Figure 5C: The NF186 staining is not convincing at all. This needs to be improved. At the moment, it appears very unspecific. Co-localization with another nodal component or another antibody with a less non-specific signal could help. In addition, the resolution of the images shown in Figure 5B is not good enough and should also be improved. The mbpa:tagrfp-caax does not help much either. It would be better to use an antibody to detect MBP or Neurofilament, for example.

7. Figure 6A: Again, the staining here for C5b-9/C5b-8 is not convincing. First, the signal is very low and we don't see much. Second, it is not clear whether the authors permeabilized the tissues or not (this information does not seem to be given in the Material and methods section). C5b-9/C5b-8 should be localized at the cell surface, so a cross-view should be added to the longitudinal view to demonstrate the membrane localization.

8. Discussion: This part does not really discuss in depth the main claimed findings of the study and does not discuss the potential implication of the new findings in relation to the CD59 human deficiency and neurological dysfunctions resistant to treatment by complement inhibitors. This part thus appears incomplete.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This is an interesting and relevant manuscript and nice work, and everyone in the field should benefit from reading it. My congratulations! I have just a few observations that the authors may want to consider for their revision

-As CD59 is only one out of several factors affecting Schwann cell development (GPCRs, ECM, transcription factors,.…), I feel phrasing that CD59 'orchestrates' SC development (in the title) may be a little too strong. 'Regulates', maybe?

-Some letters and numbers are too small to be deciphered in Figure 1 Suppl 1 A, C1, C2 and D

-Image quality is comparatively poor in Figure 1 Sup1 A, B1, B2, B3. This may be just in my PDF copy, but if not the authors may want to search for ways to improve them.

-In Figure 1 Sup1 D legend, I suppose the authors mean 'myelinating OLCs', not 'mouse OLCs'

-Page 26, Line 226-227, I suppose the authors mean 117 AA, not 177 AA

- In case suitable samples and antibodies are available, Figure 3 would benefit from Western blot validation of the lack of CD59 in the zebrafish line.

-Figure 4 F, the authors may want to consider if these are truly representative images. The difference is not easily spotted.

-Why not switch Figure 4 S2 and Figure 4 S1? It may possibly fit better with the line of arguments. Not essential, just a suggestion.

-Figure 5 A, can the authors please double-check if these are truly representative images? I am asking because the axon diameters seem to differ in the mutants as judged by the example images. Are there enough suitable samples to quantify axonal diameters? Is it possible to say if axons are normally sorted out of bundles, i.e. to quantify the numbers and diameters of axons in bundles? Sorting defects are common pathology in the PNS, at least in mammals.

- In case suitable samples and antibodies are available, Fig6 would benefit from a Western blot for the complement. Not an essential revision

-Related to Fig7, in case suitable samples are available it would be interesting to see TEM of myelinated axons and nodes after Dexamethasone treatment. Not an essential revision, just interesting

- In case the required samples are available, it would be interesting to see some examination of adult WT vs mutant zebrafish. Not an essential revision, again.

results.result: cd59 is highly expressed in developing myelinating glial cells across species. RNAseq data shows cd59 expression in zebrafish oligodendrocyte lineage cells (2145.1 ± 1215.1 TPM) and Schwann cells (40.1 ± 16.3 TPM) at 72 hpf, with minimal expression at 36 hpf (0.0 ± 0.0 TPM). Expression increases from neural crest cells through SC precursors, immature SCs, pro-myelinating SCs, and mature myelinating/non-myelinating SCs. In oligodendrocytes, cd59 is expressed near myelination onset and primarily in mature OLs rather than OPCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 provide quantitative RNAseq data with error estimates, and claims C27-C31, C33-C35 are supported by multiple published datasets and citations. The temporal and cell-type-specific expression patterns are consistently documented across zebrafish, rodent, and human studies with appropriate references to figures and supplementary data.

results.result: Based on expression patterns, Cd59 may be important during early SC development and in mature myelinating cells, but likely does not play a role in early OLC development, potentially influencing only mature myelinating OL function.
results.evaluation: These are inferences (C32, C36) drawn from expression data rather than functional experiments. The use of 'may be' and 'could influence' indicates speculation. While the expression patterns support these hypotheses, no functional data is provided to confirm these roles, making the claims uncertain.

results.result: cd59 RNA expression was verified in OLCs and SCs at 3 dpf using CISH and FISH, with expression largely confined to developing myelinating glial cells beyond heart and pancreas. cd59:tagrfp labels OLs and SCs with myelin-like processes. Expression is heterogeneous: cd59 is not expressed in NCCs at 24 hpf, shows sporadic expression at 36-48 hpf, and robust expression at 72 hpf in pLLN SCs. Only 4.4-9.4% of pLLN SCs express cd59:tagrfp, and cd59 is absent in spinal motor nerve SCs and MEP glia.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C50 are supported by multiple experimental approaches (CISH, FISH, in vivo confocal imaging) with specific references to figures. The quantitative data for subset expression (C47: 4.4 ± 1.5% to 9.4 ± 3.8%) is provided with error estimates. The heterogeneous expression pattern is consistently documented across developmental stages and cell types.

results.result: Two cd59 mutant alleles were generated: cd59uva48 has a 15 bp deletion at the exon 2-intron 2 splice site producing multiple splice variants with early stop codons, resulting in severely truncated proteins (10-48 AA) lacking the Ly6/uPAR domain and GPI-anchor signal sequence. cd59uva47 has a 6 bp deletion producing a single transcript with a 117 AA protein missing two amino acids in the N-terminal signal sequence. Both homozygous adults are viable with no anatomical, behavioral, or reproductive defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 are supported by molecular characterization including RT-PCR, Sanger sequencing, and phenotypic observations. The genomic and transcript mutations are documented with specific sequences and predicted protein structures. However, C53-C54 are inferences about protein function based on sequence analysis rather than direct protein functional assays, though the reasoning is sound given the loss of critical domains.

results.result: Wildtype and cd59uva48 mutant larvae both have sox10, mbp, and krox20-positive SCs along the pLLN at 72 hpf, indicating Cd59 is not necessary for SC genesis or expression of genes for SC maturation and myelination. cd59 expression is significantly reduced in mutant SCs (Figure 3J), suggesting mutant RNA undergoes nonsense-mediated decay. cd59uva48 mutants can serve as a loss-of-function model for studying Cd59 in developing SCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by CISH data showing presence of SC markers. C61 provides quantitative evidence of reduced cd59 expression. C62 is a reasonable inference based on the presence of premature termination codons and reduced RNA levels, though direct NMD pathway analysis is not shown. C63 is a justified conclusion given the molecular characterization, though the lack of protein-level confirmation (acknowledged by authors) introduces some uncertainty about whether this is a true null allele.

results.result: cd59uva48 mutant embryos and larvae have significantly more SCs compared to wildtype siblings at all stages from 36 hpf (SCP stage) through 48 hpf (iSC and pmSC stages) to 72 hpf and 7 dpf (mature MSC stages). The same phenotype was observed in cd59uva47 mutants at 48 hpf, ruling out off-target effects. Cd59 functions to limit overproliferation of SCs during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data across multiple developmental stages with statistical significance (p<0.0001 for multiple comparisons). The use of a second independent mutant allele (C68) strengthens the conclusion that the phenotype is due to cd59 mutation. C69 is a well-supported inference from the proliferation data.

results.result: EdU incorporation shows increased numbers of EdU-positive SCs in cd59uva48 mutants compared to wildtypes. Time-lapse imaging reveals cd59uva48 mutant SCs undergo significantly more mitotic events than wildtype siblings between 48-55 hpf, but similar numbers of divisions between 54-75 hpf with no difference in timing of terminal division. cd59uva48 mutant larvae can terminate SC proliferation at the same developmental stage as wildtype larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by quantitative data from EdU incorporation assays and time-lapse imaging with statistical analysis. C73 is a well-supported inference showing that while initial proliferation is amplified, the mutants retain the ability to terminate proliferation normally. The temporal specificity of the proliferation defect (48-55 hpf) is clearly documented.

results.result: cd59 mutation does not affect SC death (AO and TUNEL assays), spinal cord neuron density, pLLG neuron numbers, cranial or spinal motor nerve NCC numbers, Sox10-positive cells on motor nerves, or truncal neuromast numbers. Neuronal and NCC proliferation are unaffected. The increase in SC number is not due to increased NCCs. Cd59 plays an early role in SC development by limiting proliferation, and this effect does not extend to other neural cells in the CNS or PNS.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C85 are supported by multiple negative results from various assays (AO, TUNEL, immunofluorescence) showing no differences between wildtype and mutant in cell death, neuron numbers, NCC numbers, and neuromast formation. These controls are important for demonstrating specificity of the SC proliferation phenotype. C86-C87 are well-supported conclusions from the comprehensive cell-type analysis.

results.result: cd59uva48 mutant SCs can produce myelin (shown by ISH, confocal imaging, and TEM). Myelin sheath length at 7 dpf does not vary between wildtype and mutants, with no overlapping sheaths. However, myelinated nerve volume is significantly reduced in mutants. Axon volume and cross-sectional area are unaltered. There is a nonsignificant decrease (p=0.0568) in average myelin wraps per axon relative to axon area, with no change in average axon area or total myelinated axons. The reduced nerve volume could be related to decreased myelin wraps per axon.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93, C95-C96 are well-supported by multiple imaging modalities. However, C94 reports a nonsignificant trend (p=0.0568), and C97 is speculative inference connecting this trend to the nerve volume reduction. The lack of statistical significance for the myelin wrapping defect, combined with the authors' own uncertainty about whether this is a direct or indirect effect of cd59 mutation, makes the mechanistic connection uncertain. Additional experiments would be needed to establish causality.

results.result: cd59uva48 mutant larvae have fewer discrete sodium channel clusters and NF186 clusters along the pLLN at 7 dpf. NF186 and sodium channels always colocalize in wildtype larvae, confirming these are bona fide nodes of Ranvier. cd59uva48 mutant larvae do not form nodes of Ranvier normally.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data with statistical significance. C100 provides validation that the quantified structures are indeed nodes of Ranvier through colocalization analysis. C101-C102 are well-supported conclusions, though the authors appropriately note uncertainty about whether this is a direct effect of cd59 mutation or secondary to SC overproliferation or myelin changes.

results.result: Cd59 is best known as a complement inhibitory protein that protects healthy cells from lytic death by binding C8 and C9 to prevent MAC formation. CD59a is neuroprotective in multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica models. Beyond complement inhibition, Cd59 can facilitate vesicle signaling in pancreatic cells, suppress cell proliferation in T cells and smooth muscle cells, and orchestrate proximal-distal cell identity during limb regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C112 are established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide important background context for interpreting the study's findings. All claims are properly referenced to published literature.

results.result: Patients with congenital CD59 deficiency or germline paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria present with polyneuropathies during infancy and continue to have nervous system dysfunction throughout their lives. Neurological symptoms persist even with complement inhibition treatment. This indicates CD59 has an additional role in the developing nervous system beyond complement inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by multiple clinical case study citations. C116 is a reasonable inference from the clinical observations, particularly the persistence of neurological symptoms despite complement inhibition. This provides important clinical context and motivation for the study.

results.result: cd59uva48 mutant larvae have more MACs (C5b8-C5b9) localized to sox10:megfp-positive SC membranes compared to wildtype controls at 55 hpf, indicating developing SCs are no longer protected from complement in cd59uva48 mutants.
results.evaluation: C117 is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data (p<0.0001) shown in Figure 6A-C. However, the authors themselves note this requires further investigation to confirm the quantification reflects increased MAC formation. C118 is an inference that, while logical, requires additional validation. The antibody specificity and whether the signal truly represents functional MAC formation versus non-specific binding needs confirmation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this as preliminary evidence.

results.result: Dexamethasone (Dex) treatment restores SC numbers to wildtype levels in cd59uva48 mutant embryos and significantly reduces SC numbers in wildtype larvae, indicating developmental inflammation plays a role in homeostatic SC development. EdU incorporation in cd59uva48 mutant SCs returns to wildtype levels with Dex treatment, confirming Dex suppresses SC proliferation. Dex also reduces EdU incorporation in wildtype SCs, showing it can alter homeostatic SC proliferation. Developmental inflammation aids in normal SC proliferation and is amplified when cd59 is mutated.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120, C122, C124 are supported by quantitative data from Dex treatment experiments with statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests). C121, C123, C125-C127 are well-supported inferences from the experimental data. However, the authors appropriately note that future work is needed to rule out other effects of glucocorticoid signaling and to determine if sublytic MAC formation directly affects SC proliferation in vivo. The rescue experiments provide strong evidence for the role of inflammation, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Dex treatment dramatically increases sodium channel clusters in cd59uva48 mutant larvae to wildtype levels and restores mutant nerve volume to wildtype levels at 7 dpf. Inflammation-induced SC proliferation contributes to perturbed myelin and node of Ranvier development. Inhibition of developmental inflammation can protect nerve development after cd59 mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by quantitative data from immunofluorescence and confocal imaging with Dex treatment, showing statistical significance. C130-C131 are well-supported conclusions from the rescue experiments. However, the authors appropriately note this is preliminary evidence and acknowledge uncertainty about whether the effects are direct consequences of Cd59 dysfunction, secondary to SC overproliferation, or indirect effects of developmental inflammation. The rescue of both proliferation and structural phenotypes with Dex treatment provides strong support for the role of inflammation.

results.result: Developmental inflammation stimulates SC proliferation and this process is balanced by Cd59 to ensure normal SC and myelinated nerve development.
results.evaluation: C132 is the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. It is well-supported by the comprehensive data showing: (1) cd59 expression in developing SCs, (2) SC overproliferation in cd59 mutants, (3) increased MAC formation in mutants, (4) rescue of proliferation and structural defects with anti-inflammatory treatment. However, the authors appropriately acknowledge that the precise mechanism linking Cd59, MACs, and SC proliferation requires further investigation, and alternative explanations involving other glucocorticoid signaling effects cannot be completely ruled out.

results.result: Patients with CD59 dysfunction develop neurological dysfunction during early childhood, yet the function of Cd59 in the developing nervous system is currently undefined.
results.evaluation: C3 is supported by clinical literature citations. C4 accurately represents a knowledge gap that motivates the study. These claims provide important context for the research question.

results.result: The study demonstrates cd59 is expressed in a subset of developing SCs, developing SCs proliferate excessively in cd59 mutants, nerves may have reduced myelin volume, altered ultrastructure, and perturbed node of Ranvier assembly, complement activity is elevated in mutants, and inhibiting inflammation restores SC proliferation, myelin volume, and nodes of Ranvier to wildtype levels. This identifies Cd59 and developmental inflammation as key players in myelinating glial cell development, highlighting collaboration between glia and the innate immune system.
results.evaluation: These are summary claims from the abstract that are supported by the detailed experimental results described in the manuscript. C7-C9 appropriately use 'may' to indicate some uncertainty about the myelin and node phenotypes, which is consistent with the nonsignificant myelin wrapping result and the authors' discussion of whether these are direct or indirect effects. C14-C15 are well-supported overall conclusions from the study.

results.result: Myelin is a specialized lipid-rich membrane that insulates axons to enhance neurotransmission and preserve axon health. It is produced by Schwann cells in the PNS and oligodendrocytes in the CNS. Normal myelin development facilitates an efficient nervous system ensuring precise motor, sensory, and cognitive function. Impaired myelination leads to neurological dysfunction causing severe physical and intellectual disabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are established knowledge properly supported by citations. These provide essential background context for understanding the importance of the study. All claims are appropriately referenced.
